item.title: 10 Underrated Yu-Gi-Oh Cards From Beyond the Brave You Need to Try
item.description:
Yu-Gi-Oh!|competitive

10 Underrated Yu-Gi-Oh Cards From Beyond the Brave You Need to Try

Look past The Great Gallant Bandit to find some really neat tech.

By Hanko Chow

|

Published Oct 21, 2026

|

9 min read

Copy Link
TCGplayer Series:

It's hard to top the last core booster set with Chaos Origins introducing Extended Art variants in a main set as well as the meta-defining Light and Darkness Ritual archetype. With that being said, Beyond the Brave has a tough crowd to please, especially since it features Joey and his Dark Time Wizard strategy. There's definitely a gap between the power level of these sets but The Great Gallant Bandit is here to hold down the fort!

10 Underrated Cards You Missed From Beyond the Brave

Everyone wants a piece of The Great Gallant Bandit, but don't let one card take all of your attention away from the other interesting archetypes - most of them are viable in Genesys! Today, I'll quickly go over what bulk cards you should look into and keep an eye on in case they have more potential in the near future!

#10 Cartoon Shade

This little Illusion has some interesting features. From being a new Illusion type monster that can be searched by Gazelle the King of Mythical Claws or Nightmare Apprentice to being a "Toon" monster, it's just a matter of time before some decks will feature Cartoon Shade as some sort of bridge to search for another card.

As of right now, there aren't that many fantastic Ritual monsters that Cartoon Shade can search for aside from maybe Herald of Ultimateness, Futsu no Mitama no Mitsurugi or Cyberse Code Magician, but it might find a home in Drytron since all of their monsters are 2000 ATK monsters that cannot be Normal Summoned/Set.

#9 Spell Shattering Sword

Another Spell is added to the Light and Darkness Ritual lineup. Spell Shattering Sword is pretty strong as disruption since it can either destroy all Face-Up Spells your opponent controls, acting not only as a niche board wipe but also possibly preventing a Continuous, Field Spell or Pendulum from resolving an effect, or it can be a monster negate while dropping their ATK to zero.

Combined with the power of Chaos Magical Hats, you have a pretty strong lineup. By setting Spell Shattering Sword, Chaos Mystic Box and perhaps Waking the Dragon with the effect of the Hats, you're highly likely forcing your opponent to destroy one of them to trigger their awesome effect. While Spell Shattering Sword doesn't summon a monster, it'll go after another random card in your opponent's hand instead.

#8 Clown Crew Cappello

The latest Clown Crew member has joined the gauntlet, and with it, another method for the deck to summon out bodies or search certain cards. Most importantly, Clown Crew Cappello is a Pendulum that, when tributed, allows you to shuffle all Pendulums from the field and the Face-Up Extra Deck back to the Main Deck (or face-down Extra Deck for specific monsters). For some reason, Cappello doesn't shuffle back Pendulums from the graveyard like the other Clown Crew members do for their respective card type. Perhaps the designers never considered that Pendulums can go to the graveyard pretty often.

The main purpose of Clown Crew Cappello is its Pendulum Scale effect, which can send any non-Pendulum Clown Crew card from your deck to the graveyard. All of the Clown Crew Traps are the most useful ones to send, with Clown Crew Finale's tributing something to search another, Clown Crew New Face placing itself and Clown Crew Soiree Operations giving Clown Crew another Tribute Summon during any Main Phase. If you already have access to Clown Crew Malabarisme and Clown Crew Biancaviso, I think sending Clown Crew Soiree Operations could be very ideal to help give you more potential Tribute Summons!

After you tribute Cappello, whether it be from the field or hand, you can trigger its effect to summon one other Clown Crew member from your Deck or Extra Deck, giving you more ways to put out bodies. Another important note is that Clown Crew Cappello is a Level 4 monster which gives the deck another monster to Tribute Summon for in case you need to. While Cappello doesn't offer much on the field aside from lowering your opponent's defenses, there may be hope that they'll design another Clown Crew member to the family in the future. Another Tribute Summon would be great since only having Clown Crew Biancaviso as the Main boss monster feels pretty lackluster.

#7 and 6 Ashtra's Domain and Akasuna the Battle Ashtra

The newest archetype being introduced in Beyond the Brave is Ashtra, aSynchro-centric archetype revolving around Traps that can summon themselves as Tuners combined with these high-Level monsters that can summon themselves, reminiscent of Kashtiras.

Out of all the Ashtra cards, the first one that stands out is Ashtra's Domain since it's like a budget Solemn Accusation or Dark Bribe without giving your opponent a draw. It's a very simple generic Spell/Trap negate that can prove to be useful for any strategy. Just look at how the Dracotail Traps are used in other decks. Maybe this is just something you'll see in the Genesys format but I think for a local setting, you can probably get away with using Ashtra's Domain if you can't get Solemn Accusations. That is, until your opponents realize they can play around it by simply setting a card first before they play their Spell/Trap.

Akasuna the Battle Ashtra seems like a pretty strong card. With 3000 ATK points, an easy summoning condition and the ability to flip all your opponent's monsters face-down at the cost of another Trap card, there's so much potential for Ashtra. I just hope their next wave of support gives them a bright future.

#5, 4 and 3 New Destiny HERO or Dark Warrior cards!

HEROs is a fan favorite strategy, but that gets even better when it's Aster Phoenix's Destiny HEROs! Unlike the Elemental HEROs, Destiny HEROs focus around Dark Warriors with graveyard effects and unique boss monsters like the infamous Destiny HERO - Plasma. This time though, another boss monster gets retrained with Destiny HERO - Destro-Dogma, showcasing the classic Destiny HERO - Dogma holding the Cyclone Blade like it did in the anime!

This retrained version of Dogma is pretty cool actually since it's almost generic depending on the graveyard deck you're building. Since you can banish any three Warrior or Dark monsters to summon it from the hand or graveyard, Destro-Dogma makes sense to try in some milling Dark strategies. The 2000 effect damage plays well with the original Dogma effect but it's most important effect could be letting you Fusion Summon using monsters from your hand, field or graveyard! I can see this being a pretty neat option in Tearlaments or Lightsworns. I'll have to try and include it in a future deck.

One of the newest Fusions you can summon with Destro-Dogma could be Skyborne Blue Cularsaw! On summon, it equips either any monster from your opponent's graveyard or banishment, or a Warrior monster from your own graveyard/banishment, giving it the ability to negate a Spell/Trap by sending an Equip Card. It's a pretty neat option for Destiny HEROs but also a strong Super Polymerization option to be used against Destiny HEROs.

Speaking of Destiny HEROs and Fusion monsters, Destiny HERO - Dreadmaster has now evolved into Destiny HERO - Dreadnought Master. It can search search for any two cards that are Destiny HEROs or mention a specific Destiny HERO by name, which is pretty strong! This even gives you access to D - Force to make Destiny HERO - Plasma even better.

While you're most likely going to use Fusion Destiny to summon Destiny HERO - Destroyer Phoenix Enforcer most of the time, I wouldn't be surprised to see Destiny HERO - Dreadnought Master being summoned either since that double search can be so strong. But just like Skyborne Blue Cularsaw, this might just be another Super Polymerization target that other players will use against Destiny HERO players to beat Plasma and Destiny HERO - Destroyer Phoenix Enforcer, so make sure there's a Destiny HERO - Dark Angel on the opponent's field to prevent that from happening.

#2 CXyz Hope Chaos Barian Dragon

Umbral Horror or Number 104: Masquerade has received a ton of Barian-related support cards in Beyond the Brave, but the one that stands out to me the most has to be the new Barian boss monster, CXyz Hope Chaos Barian Dragon. Since the K9 cards make it very easy to summon N.As.H. Knight and CXyz N.As.Ch. Knight, that means you have easy access to those Number C101-107 monsters thanks to CXyz N.As.Ch. Knight. By summoning Number C101: Silent Honor DARK through the CXyz N.As.Ch. Knight's effect, you can then Xyz summon the new CXyz Hope Chaos Barian Dragon on top!

You'll probably have a ton of Xyz Materials by the time you get to summon CXyz Hope Chaos Barian Dragon which will give it a ton of ATK points. But most importantly, the continuous effect will be live to prevent the opponent from using their search effects. Similar to Thunder Dragon Colossus or DoomZ Destruction, this one-sided Mistake may just be K9's newest end board piece to floodgate the opponent out of their deck.

#1 Elemental Saga Doriado

Another Secret Rare that should be sought after for combo shenanigans has to be Elemental Saga Doriado. It can be easily searched via Rciela, Sinister Soul of the White Forest and gives the user the ability to reborn any monster as long as you have the required attributes. Then you also get to summon another monster with a different attribute from your Deck! It's important to note that for some reason, they decided to also make Elemental Saga Doriado's effect something neither player can respond to, which makes it not lose out to something like Ghost Belle & Haunted Mansion, Dominus Impulse or D.D. Crow.

We should be glad that Protectcode Talker, Magicians' Souls and Zenna's Deceiving Doll Maidens got banned recently as otherwise this would be another tool to send off Magicians' Souls and then add back later with Firewall Dragon to summon whatever you sent off the Doll Maidens later on. I'm sure there's probably another combo to utilize Elemental Saga Doriado in the Fairy Tail or Magistus Spellcaster combo deck. By using Summon Sorceress and either Endymion, the Crescent Magistus to equip and return the Doriado to the hand or Charmer Quartet in Bloom to summon it, it's just a matter of how many Attributes you can have in rotation to make Doriado live.

Braving the Beyond

Some might tell you that Beyond the Brave is more like a Genesys set than Advanced, which is partially true considering how the meta is forming with the power level of the newer cards. But compared to how other core sets have done before, I think Beyond the Brave still has its merits especially with how popular the Genesys format is.

On the other hand, the new Angelechy cards are proving themselves to be very meta relevant in both Advanced and Genesys so those cards might just hold up the value of this set alongside The Great Gallant Bandit. I personally am also excited to play with them since they do offer a pretty unique gameplay and resolving Angelechy Opening to e4 on the opponent's first turn is pretty crazy.

item.title: An Honest Review of the FaB 3.0 Announcement
item.description:
Flesh and Blood|news|opinion

An Honest Review of the FaB 3.0 Announcement

The biggest Flesh and Blood upheaval in the last five years just dropped... and Scott has some mixed feelings about it.

By Scott Mines

|@HowlingMines
|

Published Oct 26, 2026

|

12 min read

Copy Link
TCGplayer Series:

The announcements just aren't slowing down for the team at Legend Story Studios. Normally, you'd expect to see these things banked up for the keynote at the World Championship in November, but we've already seen a brand new set and an exclusive reveal for an upcoming product this week and somehow that's just the beginning.  

You're telling me that we've also got sweeping changes that'll define the future of Flesh and Blood at every level of the game for years to come? What on earth are they saving for that keynote?! 

That's right. The announcement lovingly christened "FaB 3.0" graced our screens back on October 20th to mixed reactions from fans and collectors alike. Honestly? That's no surprise — it was a similar story when FaB 2.0 deployed back in 2022.  It's an absurd amount of information to process in one chunk with little-to-no clarification or explanation for the plans revealed. That leaves folks confused and concerned amongst the excitement while they wait for further clarity on these changes.  

While I feel somewhat obligated to discuss these changes, I also feel the need to throw in a disclaimer on this one. I am just one individual. My opinions do not necessarily reflect those of TCGplayer or LSS.  

This line gets a little blurred sometimes because I work directly with both companies, but I want to be clear on this one: I do not have access to any additional information about this announcement than the public, and these thoughts, feelings and hopes are mine and mine alone. Don't go reading into anything too much, okay?  

With all of that said, let's dive into the meat and potatoes of FaB 3.0. 

The Spirit of the Announcement

The announcement begins with a small blurb carefully placed beneath the subtitle "The next era of Flesh and Blood"  

It reads as follows:  

"Flesh and Blood was created to bring people together in the flesh and blood through the common language of playing great games. That purpose has not changed. As the game and its community have grown, we have continued to learn how our products, tournaments, and local play programs can better serve the people who make Flesh and Blood what it is: players, collectors, and local game stores.

FAB 3.0 is the next evolution of that journey.

Beginning in 2027, we are making a series of changes designed to improve the experience of opening and playing with Flesh and Blood products, make the World Tour more rewarding, and create stronger reasons to play at your local game store throughout every season."

This summary gives us the three bullet points (and three variants of each) that we'll be using to analyze this announcement. How does each change manage to: 

  • Improve the product experience for players/collectors/local game stores
  • Improve the World Tour experience for players/collectors/local game stores
  • Improve local play programs from players/collectors/local game stores 

There will always be more nuisance to these things. After all, Legend Story Studios is a business. They're looking to make money and continue their mission into the future, and that will naturally butt heads with the wishes of you or I from time to time. I feel that by using their stated intentions to inform my personal opinions, we can create a fair analysis of the level of success. 

Product Changes

Beginning with Set 22 (so not Outbreak, for those who already threw in your pre-orders), Flesh and Blood booster packs will move from two non-foil Rare or higher cards per pack to one.  

Much like the majority of the community, my immediate reaction to this change was pretty negative. If the goal is to improve the product opening experience, surely taking away a card of value isn't the way to do it? I've said the same things about "fun-sized" candy for years — there ain't nothing fun about less candy

Despite that, I couldn't shake the fact that this change was being portrayed as positive. As a result, I attempted to rationalize how this could be seen as a good thing that had been poorly communicated. Upon reading a little further, I found myself fixating on the phrase "gives our designers more freedom to make Rare cards more distinctive, impactful and exciting"  

It's no secret that most people don't look at the majority of each pack they open. Similarly, most Rare cards are already in the bulk box before they've had a moment to breathe. While Silver Age has done a reasonable job of increasing value and demand for Rare cards, the rarity has reached a point where it feels anything but rare. I agree that changing that would be a good thing.  

The most popular complaint in the community always revolves around cost-of-entry, so imagine if this change allowed some of the less powerful/generic Majestics we're used to seeing to be pulled down to Rare? You'd remedy some of that cost, increase the average value of a Rare and make the average pack more exciting. That'd be a win.  

As LSS mentions themselves, this would also be a boon to Booster Draft. Individual Rares appearing at a lower frequency should increase the replay value of a draft format and flatten the disparity between the most powerful and least powerful decks. That's a meaningful improvement for both the World Tour and Local Play programs that include draft, so I'd consider it a win. 

We also received confirmation that there are no plans to create new Fabled gems, and the Fabled rarity will be retired in favor of unique artwork, printing techniques, and alternative tools like serialization. We previously learned this at Pro Tour Las Vegas earlier this year, so no big surprises here. Legend Story Studios do not want collectability to go away, but it's clear that $400 playables with no lower rarity were not the way to do it. This was a slam dunk for me in Vegas, and it's still a slam dunk now.  

Overall? This one needs time. I firmly believe that cards like to Turn to Mindfire were already hinting at what to expect from Rares going forward. If we can pull most of the power in a deck into a lower rarity to both bring down the price and make boosters more enjoyable, I'm all about it. If I continue to chuck my Rares into a bulk box, this change can only be seen as negative. 

Premier Play Changes

In 2027, the World Tour will be focused on fewer but bigger events. This includes both the experience and available rewards for players. This is all being done in an effort to make every World Tour weekend bigger, better and less "missable" than they may have been seen as previously.  

It may surprise you to hear this, but I think this is a good thing. While it's less work for me in the booth (and I loved having something to watch/play on the big stage every weekend), I won't pretend that attendance numbers hadn't been on my mind. There are many factors to this, but part of the equation was the frequency of events available in every region — you don't feel bad about missing a Calling in favor of something else if there's another one just like it on your doorstep within two weeks.

The cash prizes are the flashiest part. $40,000 weekends at each Calling, $240,000 Pro Tour weekends and an eye-watering $500,000 of cash prizing across the World Championship weekend is big game. I'd think you'll be hard pressed to find anybody complaining about this.  

My only worry comes from making sure there are still enough events. This all sounds fantastic until I begin to fail at getting tickets to the limited number of Callings I can play. I checked out on One Piece simply because I was never able to get a ticket to play. I don't want to see the same thing happening over here.

The second part of the puzzle is the changes to prize cards at the highest level of organized play. While Gold Foil cards have served an important role in the history of Flesh and Blood, I had a feeling that this change was coming after we began to see extended art treatments exclusively used on them in an attempt to increase desirability. Similarly, we've had two seasons of Marvel prize cards for Callings already. It was a matter of time.  

It just doesn't make sense to have Marvel cards as the pinnacle of your collectability in-set and not adjust your prizing to match. I would admittedly like to see Gold Foils remain at some level (they are still available at National Championships for another year, but I'd love to see them stay there as a National-exclusive prize, frankly) but I won't be complaining when my trophy cards look more prestigious.  

Finally, Day 2 competitors at Calling, Pro Tour and World Championship events will receive an exclusive seasonal prize card stamped with the corresponding logo. This is long overdue in my opinion and I'm a big fan of the change, albeit a little less so because I think the stamp is kind of ugly. Ultimately, that's subjective. The concept itself is sound, and this is just additional EV for competitive players — they may even look better in person!  

In-Store Play Changes

This might be the element of these changes that affects most people, so it definitely got the most attention from me. Legend Story Studios believes that each season of Flesh and Blood should feel like a cohesive, non-stop journey — something I would argue is even more important with less premier play events. There always needs to be something going on.  

The goal is to create a rhythm. Each season begins with Limited in the form of a World Premiere, Pre-Release and Limited Pro Quests that allow players to leverage the skills they learned about a new set during that window. This is bookended by the Pro Tour, which features both Limited and Classic Constructed, serving as the perfect through-point to Pro Quest and Battle Grounds events for that format. The story ends with Silver Age at the Skirmish level before the journey begins anew.

This seems great. I love the idea of the local game store becoming such a focal part of the competitive season, and I love connecting the set release to the Pro Tour with this road of events. This feels clear and concise. I don't have any notes here.

Additionally, being qualified for a Pro Tour no longer prevents a player from participating in upcoming Pro Quest events. Nobody should be punished for previous successes in their non-preferred format by no longer being able to play the game. As a result, I think this change is good, but the changes that come as a result of it may not be.  

First and foremost: getting tickets to the slightly decreased number of Pro Quests was already a problem. I've got a home country Pro Tour at the start of next year, yet I found myself with only two chances to qualify because events were either capped at 24 players during the limited portion (stores don't want to hire another judge) or selling out during the Classic Constructed portion for stores that can barely seat more than that.  

I'd like to see this remedied with expectations for the organizers hosting these events. If we're dialing the number of events offered, these stores really need to be able to host 64+ players comfortably. If the only Classic Constructed Pro Quest within three hours of me can only seat 16 players while the whole country is eligible to play it, I'm going to have a bad time.  

Similarly, I'm told that US territories struggle with superteams travelling far and wide to sweep up prizing and concede their teammates into qualifying positions. While the former is less of an issue in Europe, we do struggle with the latter. I worry that this change incentivizes friend groups to travel to additional events once qualified to collude for qualifications in a world with less Pro Quest events overall. Sadly, I don't have a great solution to remedy that problem right now.  

The last point is a real stickler for me. Why doesn't the invite pass down? If we're expecting pre-qualified players to be joined by a predetermined amount of newly qualified players, it's not a numbers issue. Why are we setting an invite on fire? Out of spite? I'd love some more insight on this point specifically because I simply don't understand.

Gem Pack Changes

I've chosen to separate this little tidbit off by itself because it's the topic I've seen the most confusion about. Starting with the Outbreak season, new GEM Packs will arrive at local game stores during the middle of each play season. As of Set 22, they will include new tournament-legal cards for selected legacy heroes, similar to the expansion slot.  

LSS frames this as a commitment to local game stores, providing a reason for players to return and reconnect with their community as the season develops. I agree that it will do this. Stores deserve that type of targeted support. My concern comes from those new tournament-legal cards.  

If "Legacy" heroes mean heroes who have ascended to Living Legend, I have no qualms here. If it means heroes that were not in the most recent set, we may have some problems. This change will reward stores who crack these packs for themselves early if these cards are hotly contested for upcoming Classic Constructed events, selling the cards while they're inflated and expensive. That would universally suck.  

To be blunt, these cards are going to be very expensive if they impact the upcoming constructed season. Not everybody has a local game store. Those that do won't open all that many GEM packs each week. Getting these cards has the potential to be a nightmare and it worries me.  

If we're increasing GEM pack supply or providing other ways to acquire non-premium versions of these cards, I'd love to hear about it. Maybe legality is held off until the Pro Quest season following the packs arrival is complete? Either way, I want to hear more. As it stands, I think this stance is a little cursed, and I'd like to see it revisited. 

In Summary

Overall, there's some positives and negatives here for me. Thankfully, most of those negatives have the potential to become positive with some further explanation or a little iteration. Legend Story Studios have earned the breathing room to demonstrate that their plan is a boon for the wider Flesh and Blood community at large, so I'm more than happy to give it to them. We'll see if they stick the landing in Set 22.  

If you'd like to check out the full announcement for yourself, you can do so here. There's even a snazzy graphic that explains all the changes in one succinct square.  

That said, I'm eager to hear what you think here. FaB 3.0 is a big deal that has clearly had a world of consideration put into it, but everybody is going to have a different take based on their personal positioning to the stakes. Let me know over at @HowlingMines on X (formerly Twitter) or @howlingmines.com over on Bluesky!  

Alternatively, give my other work here on TCGplayer a peek if you'd like another slice of everything nice about your favorite game.

But until next time. I've been HowlingMines, you've been amazing!

Stay safe out there — and happy gaming!

item.title: Top 5 Best Pokémon TCG Cards From Delta Reign
item.description:
Pokémon|competitive

Top 5 Best Pokémon TCG Cards From Delta Reign

Rayquaza is amazing, but have you seen this spicy bird?

By Natalie Millar

|@nataliem9999
|

Published Oct 27, 2026

|

4 min read

Copy Link
TCGplayer Series:

Hello everyone! Delta Reign is almost here and with the new expansion we have some new cards to talk about! This set does introduce the new split Stadium mechanic which pushes for stronger Stadiums at the cost of having to play both halves of the Stadiums from your hand, and outside of these there are a bunch of strong cards!

The Best Cards From Delta Reign

Honorable Mention

Aarune is a spiritual reprint of Scott from EX Emerald, which saw a bunch of play back in the mid 2000s. Aarune is a very slow card; using your Supporter for turn to only find other Supporters and Stadiums is generally very weak in the Pokémon TCG, but if a deck is intending to be slow then Aarune can be a very strong partner for it. Slower control decks generally rely heavily on Supporter cards for their strongest effects, and since you can find Aarune from another Aarune, the best way to use this card will likely be from chaining them together. Another aspect of Aarune is that you can use it alongside the new split Stadiums, making them significantly easier to put in play. Aarune is very slow and will be unlikely to be played in normal attacking decks, but has potential in slower, more controlling lists.

#5 Tasty Rice Ball

Jumbo Ice Cream has seen a bunch of play in slower control decks such as Crustle and Kangaskhan/Boufallant, and Tasty Rice Ball is a very similar card. The first Tasty Rice Ball only heals 30 from your active Pokémon, but  each subsequent Tasty Rice Ball heals an additional 30, with the final Tasty Rice Ball healing 120 damage. If you use all four Tasty Rice Ball throughout the game you heal 300 damage, and while this is less than the 320 you would heal from Jumbo Ice Creams, you can use Tasty Rice Ball while your active Pokémon has less than three Energy attached. I'm not currently expecting Tasty Rice Ball to surpass Jumbo Ice Cream, but I think it could supplement it for additional healing.

#4 Adventuring Lantern

Earthen Vessel was one of the strongest cards in the format for a long time, and while Adventuring Lantern is not as good as Earthen Vessel was, it's still a very strong card. Many decks want access to Energy, and while you can only use Earthen Vessel for Fire and Lightning Energy, it's still a powerful card. Any deck that uses either type of Energy can likely consider including Adventuring Lantern, as the additional type can be used for Colorless Energy costs. Many decks also use Crispin and can use the additional type to fuel the acceleration effect on Crispin, and I also believe that Adventuring Lantern will be combined with the next card on this list.

#3 Mega Rayquaza ex

Mega Rayquaza ex is the headliner of this set and I think it has a ton of competitive potential. It's a 280 Basic Pokémon, and has the Roar of the Ruler ability that lets you look at the top four cards of your deck and attach a Basic Energy you find there to it, then Storm Emeralda does 50 damage for each Fire and Lightning Energy on your board. You do need to get to six and sometimes seven Energy in play to take big knockouts, but you can use Ethan's Ho-Oh ex's Golden Flame ability to attach extra Energy every turn and fuel Storm Emeralda. Outside of that, you can also use Crispin and multiple Mega Rayquaza, alongside Area Zero Underdepths to fuel Energy in play, and I could see Storm Emeralda quickly ramping to a point where it's taking one-hit knockouts on anything. I would expect this deck to play similarly to the current Basic Box decks, and I imagine they will include the number one card on this list as well!

#2 Legendary Pyroduct

There are a few Legendary Stadiums in this expansion, but I think the strongest one is Legendary Pyroduct. Shutting off the abilities of all evolution Pokémon is very powerful and will likely be a mainstay at some point in its lifetime. Currently, it turns off the Powerful Hand abilities of the Alakazam line, Run Away Draw from Dudunsparce, Drakloak's Recon Directive and Crustle's Mysterious Rock Inn, as well as shutting off a number of other decks in the metagame. The biggest downside of this card is that the two halves of the Stadiums are difficult to piece together, putting a big roadblock in place for playing it early. Given how powerful the effect of this card is, I believe it'll see competitive play even though it's very difficult to put into play.

#1 Talonflame ex

One of the strongest cards in the format currently is Mega Kangaskhan ex. Many decks rely on the Run Errand ability to draw tons of cards, and it also cleanly activates the Exciting Dive ability on this Talonflame ex, allowing you to put it directly into play. It has 280 HP, free retreat and for two Energy it can use Talon Hunt, which does 150 and searches your deck for two cards and adds them to your hand. This is a fantastic card for any big basic deck as it's a very strong two-Prize attacker in the early game. You set up your hand with Talon Hunt, and even facilitate a later Legendary Pyroduct alongside a Judge to disrupt any evolution deck, or just build up an attacker next turn. I would expect Talonflame ex to be slotted into many of the various big basic decks in the format and be used as a strong two-Prize attacker.

item.title: Off-Meta Minute: Amber Sapphire Princess Ramp
item.description:
Disney Lorcana|competitive

Off-Meta Minute: Amber Sapphire Princess Ramp

Don't go sleeping on this beauty!

By Scott Mines

|@HowlingMines
|

Published Oct 28, 2026

|

8 min read

Copy Link
TCGplayer Series:

I have longed to Sail the Azurite Sea since rotation. It just hasn't been the same. 

I've never been a huge Sapphire enjoyer, but something has felt criminally amiss about blue's inability to accelerate towards their haymakers. Who decided that was Amber's slice of the color pie now?! Why can't I ready eleven ink on turn five with ease anymore? That was Sapphire's whole shtick! 

Thankfully, we knew this was likely to change with the arrival of Hyperia City and the new ink drop mechanic. Suddenly, everybodyhas access to some amount of acceleration… so surely the colors that are infamous for doing so would get the really good stuff? 

Turns out, they'd been weaving the seeds throughout the last couple of sets already. 

In a format dominated by various Emerald Steel and Emerald Amber lists, there's a lot of merit to going a little bigger and overwhelming them with card quality. That merit becomes more appealing once opponents begin to throw Ink Drops around. Cards such as Another Tale to Spin and Mickey Mouse - Best in Town provide Ink Drops to both players, so you'll want to be better equipped to use them than your opponent. That begs the question: just how big can you go? 

Well, Illumineer TG_Stelfio has begun putting that question to the test with a sweet looking new decklist. This Amber Sapphire Princess brew utilizes several new cards from Hyperia City to get ahead on ink early before slamming down haymaker after haymaker. Eventually, you'll bury your opponent in so many insurmountable threats that they simply won't have a chance. 

Does clobbering your opponent with some of the sweetest voices in Disney sound like fun? I think so. Let's check out an early build of Amber Sapphire Princess Ramp. 

TG_Stelfio's Amber Sapphire Princess Ramp - Top 8 at Hyperia City Two-Case Tournament

This deck looks to pair the best pieces of the Amber Sapphire control strategy from the previous season with some powerful new princess-themed updates. It's built around the concept of landing a four-cost character one turn early, which should directly bridge you to seven ink and begin slamming down the backbreaking top end. 

As previously joked, all this early acceleration is now provided by Amber. Mickey Mouse - Best in Town starts your lore count off early and punishes opponents who are not prepared to make best use of ink drops. This card is quickly reminding me of Daisy Duck - Donald's Date as a turn one play that snowballs horrifically if left unchecked. 

Aurora - Holding Court is a little more finicky. This card can only help accelerate you towards Princess and Queen characters, but we've reached a critical mass of expensive princesses that interest this deck. Be mindful not to rely on Aurora to reach Stitch - Carefree Surfer or Hades - Infernal Schemer early or you'll be sorely disappointed. Otherwise, she's the perfect way to rush out Cinderella - Dream Come True or Belle - Snowfield Strategist and get the party started. 

Hamm - Piggy Bank has proven its worth to this style of strategy and may actually be best in slot. It'll provide you with four resources worth of ink to work with on turn three with no questions asked, and happily facilitates bigger plays if your opponent leaves it unchecked.

I was a little surprised not to see Grandmother Willow - Ancient Advisor in this list given the availability of one drop characters to play immediately, but eighteen uninkables might be just a smidge too high. Either way, something to consider if you're building the deck yourself. It's hard to believe it's not worth testing. 

Cinderella - Dream Come True will almost always be your preferred play once the first acceleration is done, because her effect becomes multiplicative with each additional princess that makes her way into play afterwards. She's also the Shift target of choice for Cinderella - Unintentional Icon, who makes up a big part of your endgame plan. Cinderella is also the only ramp effect that will dig towards your threats and filter through your hand while enacting your gameplan, making her the total package. 

Thankfully, you've got a second viable princess to accelerate into for some redundancy. Belle - Snowfield Strategist isn't quite as carefree as Cinderella, but she helps convert those early copies of Mickey Mouse - Best in Town and Aurora- Holding Court that your opponent is almost obligated to deal with into permanent ink. If they don't want to challenge your characters, you can either keep using them or challenge yourself to force them into the inkwell. Don't forget, Belle also sees herself whenever she leaves play! 

There's also a third option. Casa Madrigal - Courtyard is an annoyingly sticky location that's best resolved after you've swept away a board with Raging Storm. However, you can also choose to run it out early if you intend on playing a Moana - Curious Explorer to jump you towards Raging Storm. It's nice to have a threat that plays well with your board clear, and it will often be correct to sneak it into your curve over one of the other princesses. 

At this stage, you've entered the weird mid-game portion of the gameplan where you kinda want to continue accelerating your ink to astronomical numbers, but you may have to slow down and interact with your opponent's gameplan too. If you've got the green light to continue your nonsense, establish a copy of Moana - Curious Explorer to turn those early character and removal spells into more ink to play with. 

If you need a middle ground, the new Cinderella - Unintentional Icon is often perfect. She can shift atop your Cinderella - Ballroom Sensation to enter swinging, clearing away almost any problem on the other side. Similarly, she's great at singing Let it Go and allowing her ability to do some heavy lifting anyway. 

While her ability isn't quite as good as drawing a card while continuing to ink, the control over the top of your deck will keep your draws potent and consistent. Heck, if you find too many good things, you can rely on a copy of Minnie Mouse - Urban Visionary to pick that card back up later!

Alternatively, you may find yourself needing to slow the opponent down after a particularly potent start. Spooky Sight is a deliberate inclusion to enable this. It's significantly faster to play than a Raging Storm and happily stuffs your early accelerants into your inkwell to further progress your gameplan.

Once you've successfully built up your stockpile of ink, it's time to begin outclassing your opponent every turn with a board-defining play. Stitch - Carefree Surfer will often feel like the most powerful of these given how frequently you're playing other characters to accelerate your ink, but Hades - Infernal Schemer will be the go-to when you need to continue slowing your opponent down. Both cards have been the backbone of decks like this since The First Chapter — it should be no surprise that they're continuing to do so. 

In contrast, Minnie Mouse - Urban Visionary is the new kid on the block from Hyperia City. A 6/6 character with Ward is monstrous as a baseline, forcing opponents to throw their board into it in a desperate attempt to survive, but Minnie is so much more than that. 

Each time she ends a turn exerted, you'll be able to look into your inkwell and dredge up the best card found within. No longer do you need to fear inking Stitch - Carefree Surfer early. Cindrella - Unintentional Icon won't accidentally ink your best cards. Heck, you can even recur additional copies of Minnie! I think this card is being slept on right now and I'm excited to see it finding success early. 

The remainder of the deck is padded out with efficient removal options that can answer whatever question the opponent poses. The Horseman Strikes! and Let it Go are amongst the best spot removal in Core Constructed right now, while Raging Storm is the be-all-end-all answer to an opponent caught unprepared. 

The latter particularly shines in an archetype designed to have so much ink — it's not uncommon to fire Raging Storm off as early as turn five.

But there's one other trick hidden away in that list of actions: Ohana Means Family. One of the biggest pain points for a deck that hopes to get ahead before burying the opponent in 1-for-1 removal is card advantage. You need a way to top the tank back up after you've enacted your plan — that's part of what makes Stitch - Carefree Surfer so good. 

While it's no Rapunzel - Gifted with Healing, Ohana Means Family shines in a deck with so many high willpower characters. It actively discourages the opponent from questing by providing huge resource swings if they do, and punishes any opponent attempting to remove a big character across multiple turns. When this card effect lands for maximum value, you feel like a genius. I'm all about cards that make me feel like a genius. 

Closing Thoughts

Amber Sapphire Princess Ramp seems to tick all the boxes out of the gate: fun, powerful and packed with potential. It's a deck I'm eager to explore further as the format begins to blossom under the weight of Hyperia City. Will it be a mainstay? Who knows. I just know I'm eager to find out. 

Have further questions? Let me know over at @HowlingMines on X (formerly Twitter) or @howlingmines.com over on Bluesky! Alternatively, give my other work here on TCGplayer a peek if you'd like another slice of everything nice about your favorite game.

But until next time. I've been HowlingMines, you've been amazing!

Stay safe out there - and happy gaming!

item.title: The Biggest Price Spikes in Magic: The Gathering This Week - 10/29/2026
item.description:
Magic: The Gathering|finance

The Biggest Price Spikes in Magic: The Gathering This Week - 10/29/2026

Star Trek is coming, but a riddle of Sphinxes have other ideas.

By Corbin Hosler

|@Chosler
|

Published Oct 29, 2026

|

5 min read

Copy Link
TCGplayer Series: Movers and Shakers

The Ur-Sphinx continues to move prices.

Reality Fracture may not be here for long – the release of Star Trek is just around the corner now, along with the 2026 Magic World Championship in Atlanta – but it's been a massive hit in its short time. Week after week we've covered the price increases of Sphinxes for the popular color/type-shifted The Ur-Dragon, and this week we have a new entrant into the list. In fact, it's one of the first mythic rares I ever opened when I started playing the game, not that I ever expected it to become such a relevant card. But here we are, and up goes the price of Sphinx Sovereign.

The price of the Shards of Alara mythic rare has really taken off over the last week. Ever since its printing way back in 2008, the Esper bomb was really ahead of its time for doing its damage to each opponent – Commander (or EDH) wasn't really a huge thing back in 2008 – but it was never worth more than just a couple of dollars.

Until now. Since last week the floor has shot up on Sphinx Sovereign, and today you're looking at $10+ for a copy of the mythic rare, just the latest Sphinx to spike. For instance, Unesh, Criosphinx Sovereign has settled at around $11, with a steadying out around that price rather than a post-spike crash, and Magister Sphinx settling around $10 after its own run from bulk rare status.

But that's not all that Reality Fracture is spiking this week.

Believe it or not, this silly sorcery used to be an extremely powerful competitive Magic strategy, sometimes as a surprise out of the sideboard. Turning any random creature that your deck produces into the best – typically only – creature card in your deck wins a lot of games, and would see some 60-card action over the years. There was even a short window where Mass Polymorph was feasible.

Which also now applies to Commander, thanks to the Jace-centric Multiverse Reformed Commander deck that operates heavily in this space. As a result, the original Polymorph from way back in Mirage has run up to almost $15 for a Near Mint copy, of which there are not many.

Similarly, Divergent Transformations is spiking for the same reason. The red sorcery is a double-Polymorph printed in Commander 2016 and Commander Masters, and it fits in the same decks that Polymorph goes into – so of course it has spiked in price alongside it. Divergent Transformations is up from a bulk rare to almost $10, in the latest case of a new Commander leading to massive, nearly overnight spike in price.

A bit of a spike in the making; Timesifter's Near Mint listings have been running, and you're looking at over $10 for a clean copy of the Mirrodin artifact today. That's way up from the $3-4 it was a couple of weeks ago. Is this addition from the Polymorph-style decks or something else? I'm not sure, but either way it's a big gain on a very old card.

Another hit in the Jace decks, Nicol Bolas, God-Pharaoh is likewise climbing in price right now. The big bad from Magic's original stories, this Bolas printed in Hour of Devastation may have the highest pure power level of any of the handful of Nicol Bolas planeswalker printings. It takes free spells from opponents and was printed at a time when doing so with no strings attached wasn't nearly as common as it is today. This Bolas also comes with four abilities overall, so overall it's no surprise to see it moving in tandem with the other cards mentioned.

Nicol Bolas, God-Pharaoh is up from the $4 it was a month ago to reaching almost $10 this week. And don't look now but the Marvel Super Heroes printing of Spark Double has quietly doubled in price up to almost $8 over the last two months, with reason to believe there will be more demand for it as players flesh out their new decks.

The new aggressive face of Rakdos in Modern. These lists are huge on building in redundancy with late-game plays from its graveyard, but are not wholly reliant on the graveyard at all. It's a potent combination that keeps opponents off guard and keeps the staples in this new archetype climbing in price.

Included in that list is Nethergoyf, which this week is up to a new post-release high of $8-9, up from $4-5 a month ago. It's a drastic reversal for a card that saw some play originally after its debut in Modern Horizons 3 and had been dropping for the better part of two years.

Moonshadow, too, has climbed a bit. The Lorwyn Eclipsed mythic rare that helped enable this archetype before the turbo boost it got from Dark Matter Manipulator, has climbed in price from $15 at the beginning of the month all the way up to $22 today. At a fundamental level in Modern, Thoughtseize and Blood Moon will always find a home, and this archetype is the one that best combines those two cornerstones right now.

Fear of Missing Out has also begun to climb some in price, ticking up from $3 to $5 this week as another key piece in the aggressive puzzle the Rakdos deck can produce, and Dark Matter Manipulator seems to be settling around $4-5 after jumping from the dollar rare status it held on release week.

I'll be honest, I think it's recent cEDH success driving up the price on Shadowmoor's Knacksaw Clique. It hasn't been in a breakout Modern deck, doesn't seem to be a must-include on any recent new or popular commander, and has the quirky untap ability that they played around with in that set. That said, it seems great alongside Kinnan, Bonder Prodigy in Commander.

But no matter how it got here, Knacksaw Clique has exploded in price so I want to highlight it here before I go. It has no reprints, and the Shadowmoor copy went from $5 at the beginning of the month to close to $15 today. Shadowmoor wasn't printed a ton by today's standards, so I'm not shocked to see it spike so hard and I would expect it to at least linger at the high price point for a while to come, especially Near Mint copies.

See you next week!

item.title: The 10 Cards Everybody Wants from Delta Reign
item.description:
Pokémon|collecting

The 10 Cards Everybody Wants from Delta Reign

Rayquaza reigns supreme.

By Peter Day

|

Published Oct 29, 2026

|

7 min read

Copy Link
TCGplayer Series: The Cards Everybody Wants

The king returns! After more than a decade, Mega Rayquaza is finally coming back to the Pokémon TCG in the November 6 expansion Delta Reign.

Compared to headliners like Charizard, Rayquaza makes far fewer appearances in the Pokémon TCG, but it always leaves a huge impact. The last time we got Mega Rayquaza in cardboard form was back in the 2015 set Ancient Origins, where M Rayquaza-EX quickly became one of the most valuable cards in the Series. Rayquaza later came back in 2020's Evolving Skies, the set that defined the Sword & Shield era and the pandemic-fueled Poké-boom.

So, yeah. Collectors can't wait to open Mega Rayquaza ex, and players are nearly as excited by the prospect of unleashing its Storm Emeralda attack that can KO anything in the game.

That said, Rayquaza isn't the only beloved Pokémon getting rare, strong, and beautiful new cards in Delta Reign. As you're tearing through packs in November, keep an eye out for these heralds of the Sky-High Pokémon's majesty. These are the Pokémon cards everybody wants from Delta Reign.

Note: The Pokémon Company International has not revealed images for the English versions of all the cards in Delta Reign. For the cards below without English images, we've substituted the Japanese versions of the cards from the set Storm Emeralda, so you can enjoy the gorgeous art we're about to receive.

#10 SIR Mega Golisopod ex

Special Illustration Rare (SIR) is traditionally the most sought-after rarity in modern Pokémon sets, and Delta Reign will be no exception. While SIR Mega Golisopod ex might not be anyone's first pick at this rarity, the challenge of finding it and nagimiso's intense artwork will still make it an exciting pull.

Mega Golisopod ex also threatens a respectable 220 damage for just one Energy as long as the opponent's Active Pokémon already has damage on it. That high single-target damage pairs well with fellow Grass-type Arboliva ex, and could make Golisopod a real contender once Dragapult ex and Teal Mask Ogerpon ex rotate out of Standard in April 2027.

#9 Legendary Pyroduct

Delta Reign introduces a new mechanic to the Pokémon TCG: Legendary Stadiums.

Like Pokémon LEGEND from the HeartGold & SoulSilver Series, these Stadiums are so powerful they're split across two cards, which you have to draw and play together. The resulting Legendary Stadium still gets bumped by your opponent playing a regular Stadium, but as long as it stays in play, it can completely define a game.

Of the three Legendary Stadiums in Delta Reign, the one that players and collectors are most excited for is Legendary Pyroduct. This Stadium shuts down all Abilities on Evolution Pokémon, from Drakloak's Recon Directive to Dudunsparce's Run Away Draw to N's Zoroark ex's Trade and Dusknoir's Cursed Blast. Basic Pokémon remain unaffected, so Legendary Pyroduct slots easily into Basic Box decks, which got another helpful upgrade in Delta Reign we'll cover in #7.

Power aside, this connected artwork pair looks simply gorgeous. The magma that pours through this scene has a delightfully gloopy quality, like you're peering into a red-hot honeycomb, and I love how deftly akagi has integrated the Poké Ball symbol.

#8 IR Growlithe

This Illustration Rare (IR) is here for exactly one reason: it's really, really cute.

Many Pokémon artists have created memorable cards lately by drawing Pokémon doing the same things we're used to seeing our pets do. And it's hard to imagine more adorable pet-like behavior than waiting by the door for you to come home.

#7 Talonflame ex

Talonflame ex may be a Stage 2, but it's going straight into every Basic Box deck as soon as possible—and really, any deck that runs Mega Kangaskhan ex. That's because its Excited Dive lets you drop it onto your Bench as long as you have a Colorless Mega Evolution Pokémon ex in play.

Talonflame and Kangaskhan make a mean tag-team, with both Pokémon hitting hard, drawing or searching cards, and retreating into each other for free (as long as you have Latias ex). The shell around them can and will change as Standard evolves, but this combo will probably define at least one deck during their time in the format. 

Note that Legendary Pyroduct does not shut off Excited Dive, because Excited Dive activates while Talonflame ex is still in your hand. Block evolution decks all you want!

#6 IR Kecleon

Tomokazu Komiya's cards always make me do a double-take.

Besides being trippy and fascinating, Komiya cards have a history of being bought out by speculators. The reasonable assumption is that if a card is memorable, that also makes it desirable.

I don't know if anyone will try to target Kecleon, especially in the current market where vintage is king again and modern chase cards have been dropping across the board. Regardless, Komiya fans will be celebrating come November.

#5 SIR Zinnia's Trust

Wherever Rayquaza goes, Zinnia follows.

Zinnia cards were a big draw in previous Dragon-themed sets like Evolving Skies and Dragon Majesty, and this one will likely continue that trend in Delta Reign—especially given its Special Illustration Rare rarity.

Zinnia also works wonders with the Talonflame ex/Mega Kangaskhan ex duo mentioned above. With Mega Kangaskhan in the Active Spot and Ignition Energy attached, you can swap to Talonflame ex and move the Ignition Energy so you can attack immediately. Then you search up another Zinnia's Trust, so you can keep swapping to whichever Pokémon is less damaged while maintaining your pressure and draw power.

#4 IR Eevee

Count us lucky we got this Eevee in Delta Rein! Over in Japan, it was only available in the Eevee ex Starter Set, which has made it much harder to track down. That context will make dedicated collectors even more hungry for the English version.

Plus, you know… it's Eevee. Riding in a bag. That alone puts it in contention for the most valuable Illustration Rare in the set.

#3 SIR Raikou ex

The Legendary Beasts are still one of the most iconic and beloved Legendary trios in Pokémon history, and Raikou ex will be a must-have Special Illustration Rare for fans of this lightning-fast Pokémon.

Raikou has been underserved in terms of full-art cards in the past, so this dynamic take on the Thunder Pokémon by Oku will immediately flash to the top of the list of the best illustrations it's ever received.

#2 IR Kyogre and Groudon

Speaking of iconic trios, Rayquaza has two counterparts of its own to contend with—the other two points in the triangle that put the "delta" in Delta Reign.

Kyogre and Groudon have returned to the Pokémon TCG, this time as Illustration Rares. Normally that would put these cards below Special Illustration Rares in terms of desirability, but Nurikabe and Ryota Murayama's color-saturated artwork demands too much respect for collectors to overlook.

Kyogre and Groudon have a long history of appearing in valuable, mirrored-artwork cards. Regardless of their printed rarity, these are two Illustration Rares that no collectors will want to move on from Delta Reign without.

#1 MHR and SIR Mega Rayquaza ex

Above every other chase card in Delta Reign is the Sky-High Pokémon itself, Mega Rayquaza.

Mega Rayquaza first appeared in the Pokémon TCG more than a decade ago in Roaring Skies and Ancient Origins, the latter of which gave us one of the most expensive Rayquaza cards ever printed. Now Mega Rayquaza is back with three different versions in Delta Reign, two of which will be the rarest and most valuable cards in the set.

Mega Hyper Rare (MHR) Mega Rayquaza ex is the highest-rarity card in Delta Reign, but you probably could have figured that out just by looking at it. With its gold monochrome finish, this card practically screams "premium," and its Japanese version has a price point to match.

On the other hand, Special Illustration Rare Mega Rayquaza ex brings more colors to bear, making this illustration by Kazuki Minami feel even more intense. Given the precedent set by other Mega Evolution Series sets like Perfect Order, Chaos Rising and Pitch Black, SIR Mega Rayquaza ex will likely rise to become the most expensive card in Delta Reign as more collectors scramble to find this exclusive artwork.
